title: How do I start my own country?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how a new country can be started, beginning with a joking hypothetical about getting revenge on high school bullies by founding a nation. They cover land-based secession versus buying an island, historical examples (Rhodesia/Zimbabwe, Soviet dissolution, Yugoslavia and Tito, Kosovo), the criteria for statehood (permanent population, government, territory, ability to conduct foreign relations), the declaration of independence and UN recognition process (including the Secretary General letter and the two-thirds Security Council/General Assembly requirements), and how recognition is political. They discuss micronations, notably the Republic of Molossia in Nevada and the Principality of Sealand, a former WWII sea fort off England that Roy Bates claimed in 1967, its 1978 mercenary takeover attempt, and its de facto sovereignty status. The episode closes with a listener mail from Sarah and show housekeeping.

segments.title: Opening banter and high school revenge hypothetical
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, then Josh sets up a joking scenario in which Chuck starts his own country to get revenge on high school bullies, which leads to the question of how one actually starts a country.

segments.title: Ways to found a country: colonies, breakaway states, buying islands
segments.summary: They describe historical routes to new nations, such as a larger power colonizing and renaming territory or a colony becoming independent, and note that islands for sale exist but power supply is a problem.

segments.title: Land-based secession and the Soviet and Yugoslav breakups
segments.summary: They explain that secession from a country where you own land meets resistance, citing the Soviet Union's dissolution and Georgia, and the breakup of Yugoslavia after Tito's death, with Albanians and Serbs.

segments.title: Criteria for statehood and the Montevideo Convention
segments.summary: They list the basic requirements for a new nation: a permanent population, a government, and territory, plus a fourth criterion of being able to communicate with other states, traced to the Montevideo Convention and disputed in practice.

segments.title: Recognition politics: Taiwan and Kosovo
segments.summary: They discuss how recognition is informal and political, using Taiwan's loss of UN seat after Nixon's China outreach as an example, and Kosovo's independence recognized by the US, which was a jab at Russia.

segments.title: Declaring independence and petitioning the UN
segments.summary: They outline the steps of declaring independence and writing to the UN Secretary General, and explain that UN membership requires a two-thirds vote and can be vetoed by members.

segments.title: Natural resources, Nevada's Republic of Molossia, and recognition stakes
segments.summary: They discuss attracting investors through natural resources and currency backed by resources, then describe Molossia, a self-declared republic on Nevada land that no one recognizes, and compare it with Native American tribal independence claims.

segments.title: Principality of Sealand: history, takeover, and legal status
segments.summary: They trace Roy Bates's 1967 occupation of a former WWII sea fort off England, the 1968 incident with British Navy, the court ruling that the platform was outside English jurisdiction, Sealand's constitution, flag, currency, passports, and the 1978 takeover attempt by Alexander Achenbach that Bates reversed, ending with a German diplomat's visit as evidence of sovereignty.

segments.title: Sealand's later history, internet servers, and the Mouse That Roared
segments.summary: They cover Sealand's extension of territorial waters in 1987, the offer to sell it, its use for hosting internet servers, and a comparison with the film The Mouse That Roared.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sarah and show plugs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck read an email from long-time listener Sarah, who is turning fourteen and describes trying parkour, then mention how to contact the show and plug related content.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a brief sign-off and a promo for the Stuff from the Future video podcast.
